name: Mallet toe
aliases: DIP flexion deformity of the lesser toe

reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: A mallet toe is an isolated flexion deformity of the distal interphalangeal joint, with the metatarsophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints held in relatively neutral positions

This isolated distal deformity is the distinguishing feature against hammer toe (proximal interphalangeal flexion) and claw toe (metatarsophalangeal hyperextension plus flexion of both interphalangeal joints)
It most often affects the longest lesser toe, typically the second, where the toe tip is repeatedly buckled against the shoe
A painful callosity or corn develops at the tip of the toe or under the nail, and nail deformity may accompany chronic pressure
Repetitive footwear pressure and minor trauma are common causes, and contracture of the long flexor tendon perpetuates the deformity
Flexibility should be tested, since a passively correctable deformity may respond to flexor tenotomy while a fixed one needs joint resection or fusion
Conservative care includes deep-toe-box footwear, toe caps or crest pads to relieve tip pressure, and callus management
Surgical treatment uses flexor tenotomy for flexible deformity and distal interphalangeal arthrodesis or resection for fixed deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Mallet toe is a flexion deformity confined to the distal interphalangeal joint, produced by an imbalance favouring the long flexor tendon across that joint while the more proximal joints remain in neutral alignment. It is commonly precipitated by chronic pressure from footwear that is too short or too shallow, so that the longest toe is repeatedly forced into flexion, and by minor trauma. Over time the flexor tendon and joint capsule contract, converting an initially flexible deformity into a fixed one. The buckled distal phalanx concentrates load at the toe tip, producing a painful end-of-toe corn or callosity, subungual pressure changes, and occasionally ulceration, particularly where sensation or perfusion is impaired. Because the deformity is distal and isolated, associated metatarsophalangeal subluxation and generalised clawing are typically absent.
additionalDifferentials: Hammer toe with proximal interphalangeal flexion
Claw toe with combined metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal deformity
Subungual exostosis or nail pathology causing tip pain
Distal phalanx fracture or post-traumatic deformity
Inflammatory arthritis affecting the distal interphalangeal joint
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination localising the deformity to the distal interphalangeal joint and testing its flexibility
Weight-bearing foot radiographs to confirm the level of deformity and exclude bony lesions
Inspection of the toe tip and nail for callosity, corn, or ulceration
Assessment of the other toes and forefoot to exclude a wider deformity pattern
Vascular and neurological assessment of the toe before surgery
Inflammatory markers or serology only if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
redFlags: Ulceration or infection at the toe tip, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease
Signs of digital ischaemia that would jeopardise healing
Multiple or symmetrical toe deformities suggesting an underlying neuromuscular or inflammatory disorder
A firm, growing subungual lesion suggesting exostosis or, rarely, tumour
reference.prognosis: Mallet toe generally responds well to simple measures. Flexible deformity is often corrected by flexor tenotomy with reliable relief of tip pain, and fixed deformity does well with distal interphalangeal arthrodesis or resection. Recurrence is uncommon when appropriate footwear is maintained, though tip numbness, mild residual deformity, or persistent nail changes can occur.
pitfalls: Failing to test flexibility and performing joint resection when a simple flexor tenotomy would suffice
Missing an underlying bony lesion such as subungual exostosis as the cause of tip pain
Overlooking ulceration or ischaemia at the toe tip in the neuropathic or vasculopathic foot
Attributing an isolated distal deformity to a broader claw or hammer toe pattern and over-treating
Neglecting footwear correction so that pressure recurs after treatment
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
